title: Working at Redwood: Roles, Career Ladders, Benefits, Hiring & Onboarding, and Internal Tools
author: Priya Desai
content:
Overview:

This document is the canonical People Ops reference for: what it’s like to work at Redwood Inference, our role structure and career ladders, benefits and perks overview, the hiring and new-hire onboarding experience, and the primary internal tools you will use day-to-day. It is intended for new hires, managers, hiring interviewers, and anyone updating team-level onboarding materials.

Table of contents:
1. Working at Redwood (vision, culture, expectations)
2. Roles & Career Ladders (levels, competencies, promotion guidelines)
3. Benefits & Perks (summary and enrollment)
4. Hiring & Onboarding (processes, timelines, checklists)
5. Internal Tools (access, key guides, owners)
6. Quick contacts and ownership

1) Working at Redwood

Short intro:
Redwood is a developer-first, production-focused company. Our culture balances engineering rigor with customer empathy: we ship durable systems, run postmortems without blame, and grow by fostering autonomy and strong cross-functional collaboration. Managers are expected to enable individual growth while maintaining clarity of goals and delivering predictable outcomes.

Guiding principles (bulleted):
- Ship for production: prioritize reliability, observability, and repeatable processes.
- Customer & developer empathy: prioritize developer experience and predictable economics for customers.
- Data-informed decisions: use metrics, experiments, and clear success criteria.
- Psychological safety: run blameless postmortems, encourage questions, and welcome dissent delivered respectfully.

Day-to-day expectations for ICs and managers (short lists):
- Individual contributors: deliver high-quality code/designs, own technical scope end-to-end, write clear docs, and participate in on-call rotations where applicable.
- Managers: set clear goals, unblock teams, provide coaching and regular feedback, and coordinate cross-team dependencies.

2) Roles & Career Ladders

Overview:
We use standardized ladders to provide transparent expectations for levels across Engineering, Product, Research, and Developer Experience. Promotion decisions are competency-driven and require evidence across impact, craft, collaboration, and leadership dimensions.

Summary table (Level | Typical title | Years at level | Key expectations):
| Level | Typical title | Years at level | Key expectations |
| L3 | Software Engineer | 1-2 | Delivers features with guidance, owns small services, writes tests and docs |
| L4 | Senior Software Engineer | 2-4 | Designs subsystems, mentors peers, leads moderate-sized projects |
| L5 | Staff Engineer | 3-6 | Cross-team technical leadership, drives architecture, influences roadmap |
| L6 | Principal / Engineering Manager | 4+ | Sets multi-team strategy, owns reliability and major platform initiatives |

Competency rubrics (short bullets):
- Impact: measurable outcomes (latency, cost, uptime, revenue). Include metrics in promotion packages.
- Craft: quality of design, test coverage, monitoring, and post-deploy support.
- Collaboration: cross-functional communication, stakeholder management, and mentorship.
- Leadership: technical or people leadership appropriate to level.

Promotion process (numbered):
1. Candidate prepares a promotion packet (summary, 3-5 impact examples, supporting metrics, manager write-up).
2. Manager gathers 3-6 peer reviews using the rubric.
3. Packet is reviewed by the level calibration committee; committee provides decision and feedback.
4. If promoted, update compensation process (Finance), job description, and announce in team meeting.

3) Benefits & Perks (summary)

Core benefits (bulleted):
- Medical, dental, vision (US plans with employer subsidy; EMEA country-level benefits administered by People Ops).
- 401(k) / pension plan matching where applicable.
- Competitive parental leave (primary and secondary leave policies).
- Flexible work policy: hybrid-first with manager-agreed days on-site for cross-team work.
- Generous paid time off: 20 days PTO baseline plus public holidays; discretionary mental health days.
- Wellness stipend (annual), home office stipend for remote hires.

Perks & allowances (bulleted):
- Commuter / transit benefit or monthly allowance (region dependent).
- Learning & development budget per employee.
- Team-offsite budget and lightweight travel policy for conferences.
- Equity grants and annual refresh cycles.

Enrollment & key deadlines (numbered):
1. New hires receive benefits packet during offer acceptance and an enrollment window (first 30 days) to select plans.
2. People Ops runs a live benefits Q&A within week 2 of hire.
3. Changes outside open enrollment require qualifying life event documentation.

4) Hiring & Onboarding

Hiring philosophy (short):
We hire for curiosity, customer focus, and evidence of craft. Interviews test fundamentals, system design, production judgment, and culture add. Interviewers must follow structured rubrics and avoid off-limits questions.

Hiring process (high-level numbered):
1. Requisition & job description created by hiring manager and approved by Finance and People Ops.
2. Sourcing and screening: Recruiter screens for fit and alignment with role requirements.
3. Interview loop: typically 4-5 interviews (technical screen, systems design, cross-functional collaboration/PM or product sense, culture fit/values, and hiring manager).
4. Debrief & decision: panel uses scorecards; offer approved by People Ops and Finance.
5. Offer & negotiations: Recruiter manages offer, equity, start date, and relocations.

Interviewing best practices (bulleted):
- Use the scorecard and rubric for every candidate.
- Provide objective, evidence-based feedback (cite examples).
- Avoid hypotheticals that depend on proprietary knowledge or are biased against underrepresented candidates.

New-hire onboarding timeline (30-90 day milestones):
- Day 0-1: Offer acceptance, paperwork, and account provisioning.
- Week 1: Orientation (company mission, policies, security, benefits Q&A) and team-level onboarding plan.
- Week 2-4: Product & codebase deep dive, initial small deliverable, mentor assigned.
- Month 1-3: Ramp to full ownership, feedback checkpoints at 30 and 90 days.

New-hire checklist (numbered, manager & new hire items):
Manager:
1. Create a 30/60/90 plan and share first-week onboarding schedule.
2. Ensure accounts are provisioned (GitHub, CI, Slack, Confluence, cloud console).
3. Assign a buddy and schedule weekly 1:1s for the first three months.

New hire:
1. Complete security & compliance training in the first 72 hours.
2. Join team channels and read the team README and service runbooks.
3. Complete first small task and document learnings.

Escalation & support during ramp (bulleted):
- If access is missing after 48 hours, ping people-ops-access@redwood.com and infra-support@redwood.com.
- For blocker-related production questions, contact the on-call engineer listed in the service runbook.

5) Internal Tools: Access, Key Guides, and Owners

Primary tools (short list with one-line purpose):
- GitHub (repo hosting, code review, PR workflows) — owner: Eng Dev Tools.
- CI/CD (buildkite / GitHub Actions) — owner: Eng Infra.
- Confluence (docs & playbooks) — owner: People Ops / Eng Docs.
- Slack (team communication) — owner: IT / People Ops.
- PagerDuty (on-call and incident routing) — owner: SRE.
- Cloud console (GCP / AWS) for infra access — owner: Cloud Platform.
- HRIS and payroll (BambooHR / Rippling) — owner: People Ops.
- Expense & travel (Concur / Ramp) — owner: Finance.

Access & security guidelines (bulleted):
- All access requests follow the Access & Permissions template (see linked runbook). Requests are reviewed by resource owners and provisioned within 3 business days.
- MFA is required for all accounts with privileged access; hardware keys are recommended for engineers and managers.
- Service accounts: rotate keys and store secrets in the company KMS/Vault.

Quick how-tos (examples):
- GitHub: link your GitHub account to SSO (setup guide), create a feature branch off main/, open PRs with tests and a short changelog.
- CI/CD: write a buildkite.yml or workflow that runs unit tests and integration checks; use cached artifacts for model artifacts.
- Confluence: use the Company Handbook template for people-facing docs and the Engineering Design Doc template for design reviews.
